Each shot starts when its 'from' phrase is spoken; each cue lights its box when its 'at' phrase is spoken. Boxes are [x, y, w, h] on the 1920x1080 frame. Phrases are found in order, so a repeated phrase means the next one.

parts.title: The hook
parts.text: A supplier sends you a letter. One of your parts is being discontinued. You have thirty-four days to place one last order. After that, it's gone for good.

parts.title: The problem
parts.text: The letter is one line. The hard part is what it breaks. This one chip, A-D-U-M twelve-oh-one A-R-Z, sits inside three assemblies. Those go into five products. And those five products bring in nine million euros a year. Today, someone works that out by hand, in spreadsheets, before the date.

parts.title: What LastBuy is
parts.text: This is Last Buy. It reads the letter, traces the part through everything you build, and tells you what to buy. You give it two things. The letter, and your bill of materials. Behind it, AMD does the reading and writing. Miner U reads the scan. Gemma 4 writes the words. Both run on AMD Instinct, through AMD's Token Factory. Evolus, in our workspace called lychee, rules on the certificates. And the impact engine does the maths. That box is plain code. No model.

parts.title: A real example
parts.text: Here's a worked example. A notice from Analog Devices comes in. It's in German. Last Buy reads it and finds the part in your bill of materials. Thirty-four days to the last buy. The stock you have runs out in under five weeks. You need to buy five hundred and four thousand units. That's one point four million euros.

parts.title: Why: the graph
parts.text: Where does that come from? This graph. It starts at the chip, goes through the two boards it sits on, and up to all five products. On each path it multiplies how many go into one unit. Every line here is arithmetic. You can check it. Ask again tomorrow and you get the same answer.

parts.title: How the letter is read
parts.text: How does it read the letter so fast? A notice is a form. It ticks its own box. It prints the last-buy date next to a label. So we read the form first. If the page says it, we go straight across the top. Twenty-seven seconds. No credits. If the page doesn't say it, Evolus and Gemma fill the gap. About fifty-four seconds. Either way, you get an answer.

parts.title: The order
parts.text: The order size depends on two things. How long you keep supplying spares, and how much extra you keep as a buffer. Move them, and the number moves. Then a real person approves it. Nothing gets ordered on its own.

parts.title: Vigil
parts.text: This is Vigil, the assistant. It sits on every page. Ask it anything, across all your documents at once. Every claim ends with where it came from. The file name, if it read it. Engine, if it worked it out. And if your documents don't say, it tells you that. It doesn't guess.

parts.title: What Vigil remembers
parts.text: When a chat gets long, Vigil doesn't just summarise it. It turns it into claims, each with its source. Then it throws the chat away. Start a new chat, and it still knows the claims. A summary can't be checked. A claim with a source can.

parts.title: Cost, and the close
parts.text: A full assessment costs about a hundredth of a cent. So you can read every notice, not only the ones that look important. That's how the expensive ones get missed. Tools in this space today are databases you search. Last Buy reads the letter and tells you what breaks. Built on Gemma 4 on AMD, with Evolus. Made by Hamza Bukhari. Thanks for watching.

cues.at: reads the letter and tells you
